"Call It Stormy Monday (But Tuesday Is Just as Bad)" (commonly referred to as "Stormy Monday") is a song written and recorded by American blues electric guitar pioneer T-Bone Walker. It is a slow twelve-bar blues performed in the West Coast blues-style that features Walker's smooth, plaintive vocal and distinctive guitar work. As well as becoming a record chart hit in 1948, it inspired B.B. King and others to take up the electric guitar. "Stormy Monday" became Walker's best-known and most-recorded song.

In 1961, Bobby "Blue" Bland further popularized the song with an appearance in the pop record charts. Bland introduced a new arrangement with chord substitutions, which was later used in many subsequent renditions. His version also incorrectly used the title "Stormy Monday Blues", which was copied and resulted in royalties being paid to songwriters other than Walker. The Allman Brothers Band recorded an extended version for their first live album in 1971, with additional changes to the arrangement. Through the album's popularity and the group's concert performances, they brought "Stormy Monday" to the attention of rock audiences.

Benny Goodman made swing the standard pop music for nearly ten years, if not longer. He led a band in the early '30s that got some gigs, but didn't seem to make much of an impression, in spite of having a regular gig on a radio show that was broadcast from coast to coast called Let's Dance in 1934.

The show's sponsor, Nabisco, canceled it in early 1935, and Goodman took his band on the road, after having cut a few records in the studio. Audiences seemed mostly indifferent until they played a ballroom in Oakland California, where the kids went wild from the first notes of the first song.

Then, the next night in Pismo Beach, they flopped. Goodman and the band thought the one night was a fluke.

Until they played the Palomar Ballroom in Los Angeles on August 21st. Their first set was met with indifference, and drummer Gene Krupa supposedly said "If we're gonna die, Benny, let's die playing our own thing."
